traveler: Frida Kahlo (Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón)
title: The Blue House and the Handrail: Kahlo, the Broken Column, and the Long Return to Coyoacán
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Blue House and the Handrail

stops.name: Casa Azul, Coyoacán: the birth in the blue house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the registry gives 6 July 1907, and Kahlo herself gave 1910 for the rest of her life
stops.campa: In the house her father Guillermo built at Londres 247, painted cobalt, a third daughter is born to a German photographer and a Oaxacan mother. The barrio is Coyoacán, where Hernán Cortés kept his headquarters in 1521 and had Cuauhtémoc's feet held in fire for gold that was never found. Four centuries later the same ground carries a blue courtyard house. She will give her birth year as 1910, the year the Revolution began, and repeat it until the world takes it. The paper says 1907. She is still giving 1910 in the year she dies.
suggested_refs: The birth registry of Coyoacán, 1907; the Casa Azul at Londres 247
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (1983)

stops.name: Coyoacán: the nine months of polio
stops.date_confidence: year approximate; sources agree only on about age six
stops.campa: Poliomyelitis puts her in bed for the better part of a year. The right leg comes out of it thinner and shorter than the left, and she walks with a limp from then on. Guillermo, against every convention governing girls in Coyoacán, sets her to swimming, boxing, and wrestling to build the leg back. The children of the street call her pata de palo, peg leg. She answers with long skirts and stacked socks on the thin ankle, and the leg is not discussed. She is six, and the long skirt is already the clothing she will wear for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The Kahlo family photographs by Guillermo Kahlo, 1910s
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso: the Cachuchas and the man on the scaffold
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not established
stops.campa: She enters the National Preparatory School, one of some thirty-five girls among two thousand students, meaning to study medicine. She falls in with the Cachuchas, the caps, a reading gang of political troublemakers, and takes up with their leader Alejandro Gómez Arias. In the Bolívar Amphitheatre a fat man on a scaffold is painting the mural called Creation, and she watches him work. Fourteen years later Antonin Artaud will lecture in these same corridors, under the murals of Orozco, hunting a Mexico of ritual that this building was built to announce.
suggested_refs: Diego Rivera's mural 'La Creación', Anfiteatro Bolívar, San Ildefonso, 1922
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
artaud.journey.json (San Ildefonso, 26 February 1936)

stops.name: Calzada de Tlalpan and Cuauhtemotzín: the streetcar
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, Herrera, Gómez Arias's own letters); the commercial site fridakahlo.org dates the crash to September 1922 instead, a contradiction recorded and not resolved
stops.campa: A wooden bus carrying her and Gómez Arias home is struck broadside by an electric streetcar on the Calzada de Tlalpan. The bus does not break at once; it bends, and then it bursts. A steel handrail enters her left hip and leaves through her sex. Her spine breaks in three places, her pelvis in three, her collarbone and ribs and right leg in many. A house painter's packet of gold powder splits open over the wreck and covers her bleeding body in gold, and the people who come running cry out that the dancer must be got free.
suggested_refs: Alejandro Gómez Arias's account of 17 September 1925, printed in Herrera
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Hospital de la Cruz Roja: the first of thirty operations
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; September 1925 attested, exact day not established, and the 1925 hospital building's location is approximate because the institution has since moved
stops.campa: She is carried into the Red Cross hospital downtown, where the doctors do not expect her to live the month and her parents do not come; her mother cannot speak for weeks and her father takes to his bed. It is the first of something near thirty operations she will undergo in twenty-nine years. Afterward she spends three months immobilized in a plaster corset. She will wear corsets of plaster, leather or steel for the rest of her life, and she will paint them too.
suggested_refs: The Hospital de la Cruz Roja, Mexico City, in its 1925 premises
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Casa Azul: the mirror in the canopy
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not established
stops.campa: Flat on her back in her childhood bedroom, she asks for paint. Her father gives up his box of oils; a carpenter builds an easel that can stand over a lying body; her mother has a mirror fitted into the canopy of the four-poster so that there is always a face above her. What she can reach is herself. The first canvas is a portrait of herself in a red velvet dress, sent to Gómez Arias, who leaves for Europe the following year and does not come back to her. Medicine is finished. She paints herself again the next year, and the year after that.
suggested_refs: 'Self-Portrait in a Velvet Dress' (1926), the first painting
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Mexico City: the party at Tina Modotti's
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the exact day not established
stops.campa: She joins the Mexican Communist Party in 1927 and enters the rooms where the party keeps its evenings: Julio Antonio Mella, the Cuban exile, and the photographer Tina Modotti, whose parties gather every foreign revolutionary passing through the city. At one of them she is introduced to Diego Rivera, twenty years older, twice married, three hundred pounds, and the most famous painter in Mexico. She has watched him from a bench in the Bolívar Amphitheatre. Now she is twenty-one and has nine paintings and a spine held together with corsets.
suggested_refs: Tina Modotti's Mexico City photographs and the Communist circle of 1928
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Secretaría de Educación Pública: the paintings carried to the scaffold
stops.date_confidence: sequence attested; month reconstructed from the order of events in 1928
stops.campa: She carries three canvases into the courtyards of the education ministry, where Rivera is at work high on a scaffold, and calls him down. She does not want compliments and says so; she wants to know whether she can live by this, because she cannot live by standing up. He looks and tells her to keep going. He will write later that he was struck at once by an extraordinary force of expression, unsparing in its observation and hard as steel. He begins coming out to Coyoacán on Sundays to see the paintings, and stays for the painter.
suggested_refs: Rivera's murals in the Secretaría de Educación Pública, República de Argentina 28
sources: Diego Rivera, My Art, My Life (1960), cited in Herrera
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Coyoacán town hall: the elephant and the dove
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They marry in a civil ceremony at the Coyoacán ayuntamiento, the old Casa de Cortés on the plaza. She is twenty-two and borrows the skirt and rebozo of the family's servant for the wedding; he is forty-two and turns up late. Her mother objects and does not attend, and the household verdict passes into the language: a marriage between an elephant and a dove. Her father, who understands what an invalid daughter costs, attends and observes only that Rivera can pay the doctors. Both readings are recorded and neither is withdrawn.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Cortés, seat of the Coyoacán ayuntamiento, Plaza Hidalgo
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Cuernavaca: the Palacio de Cortés and the Tehuana dress
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from the span of Rivera's Palacio de Cortés commission
stops.campa: She resigns from the Communist Party when Rivera is expelled from it, and they go south to Cuernavaca, where he is painting the conquest and its aftermath on the walls of the palace Cortés built for himself out of the ruins of a Tlahuica temple. The commission is paid for by Dwight Morrow, the American ambassador. On the walls Cortés is a jaundiced and skeletal thing. In the garden of the borrowed house she begins to dress as a woman of the Isthmus: long skirt, square huipil, ribbons braided into the hair. She keeps to it for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: Rivera's murals in the Palacio de Cortés, Cuernavaca, 1929-1930
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Isthmus of Tehuantepec: the dress with no travel document
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Herrera notes the attribution is contested, and no primary document places Kahlo on the isthmus before she adopted the dress
stops.campa: The costume she has taken up belongs to the Zapotec women of the isthmus, who hold the markets and the money and walk through their own towns as though the towns belonged to them. That is the reason usually given. No letter, ticket, or hotel register has been found that puts her there before she began to wear it. The stop is entered as tradition rather than travel: a place that enters her life through cloth. The skirt covers the withered leg. It also puts the indigenous half of a German photographer's daughter out in the street where it can be seen, and it agrees with her husband's politics without his having to ask her for it.
suggested_refs: Tehuana dress in the Museo Frida Kahlo wardrobe, sealed 1954 and opened 2004
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (attribution noted as contested)

stops.name: San Francisco Stock Exchange: the arrival in the north
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested
stops.campa: Rivera is commissioned to paint the Luncheon Club of the Stock Exchange, and the two of them cross into the country she calls Gringolandia. She is twenty-three, walks the hills of a foreign city in Tehuana skirts, and is followed down the street. Here she meets Leo Eloesser, a surgeon who plays chamber music and sails his own boat, and who becomes for the next twenty-four years the one doctor she believes. The following year she paints Frieda and Diego Rivera, herself small beside him with her hand in his, and it hangs in the Palace of the Legion of Honor.
suggested_refs: Rivera's 'Allegory of California', Luncheon Club, San Francisco Stock Exchange
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: San Francisco General Hospital: Dr Leo Eloesser
stops.date_confidence: 1930-31; month reconstructed
stops.campa: Eloesser examines the spine, the leg, the fused sacroiliac, and advises against the knife. Rest, he tells her, a corset made properly, and posture: the surgery she keeps being offered will not give back what the handrail took. She will not always follow him, and every time she goes under a saw somewhere else she writes to tell him so. The correspondence runs to her deathbed. She paints his portrait with a model schooner behind him and gives it to him, and she will paint herself for him too, with the scars showing.
suggested_refs: The Kahlo-Eloesser correspondence, 1930-1954
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
the Eloesser-Kahlo letters cited therein

stops.name: Detroit Institute of Arts: the industrial city
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested
stops.campa: They come to Detroit for the twenty-seven panels of Detroit Industry, Edsel Ford's money paying for a Communist to glorify the assembly line. Rivera is happy in the foundries. She is pregnant, in a hotel room, in a city of smoke where she knows no one and the food tastes of nothing. She writes home that the industrial part is impressive and the rest is like an old and shabby village. The country that pays for the murals is three years into a depression, and she watches breadlines from the window of a suite the Fords are paying for.
suggested_refs: Rivera's 'Detroit Industry' frescoes, Detroit Institute of Arts, 1932-1933
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Henry Ford Hospital: the thirteen days
stops.date_confidence: attested; hospitalized until 17 July 1932
stops.campa: On Independence Day she miscarries at thirteen weeks and hemorrhages, and lies thirteen days in the hospital on West Grand Boulevard. The pelvis broken in 1925 has decided the matter. She asks for medical textbooks and drawings of a fetus so that she can paint what happened, and the hospital refuses; Rivera gets them for her. She paints Henry Ford Hospital: a naked woman on an iron bed on a plain of red earth, the factory skyline behind, six ribbons running from her belly to a fetus, a snail, an orchid, a pelvis, a machine.
suggested_refs: 'Henry Ford Hospital' (1932), Museo Dolores Olmedo
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Casa Azul: the death of Matilde Calderón
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; exact day not established
stops.campa: Word comes from Coyoacán that her mother is dying, and she travels south by train and bus for days to reach the blue house. Matilde Calderón y González dies of cancer weeks after her daughter loses the child. She goes back to Detroit and paints My Birth: a bed, a shrouded corpse of a woman from the waist up, and her own dead head emerging between the legs. She says of it only that it is how she imagined she was born. A banner scroll hangs beneath the bed in the picture with nothing written on it.
suggested_refs: 'My Birth' (1932), painted in Detroit after Matilde Calderón's death
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Rockefeller Center: the mural with Lenin in it
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed, the mural covered in 1933 and destroyed in February 1934
stops.campa: In the lobby of the RCA Building Rivera paints Man at the Crossroads and puts the face of Lenin into it. Nelson Rockefeller asks for the head to be changed. Rivera refuses and offers to balance it with Lincoln. He is paid off, the wall is boarded, and the fresco is broken to dust. She is in the room for all of it and takes the side of the wall. When they sail home in December she has had enough of the north for a lifetime, and he has not, and the argument that follows them onto the ship does not end.
suggested_refs: 'Man at the Crossroads', RCA Building lobby, destroyed February 1934
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: San Ángel: the twin houses and the sister
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the return from the United States is December 1933, the year without paintings is 1934, and the pool conflated the two
stops.campa: Juan O'Gorman has built them two functionalist boxes in San Ángel, his pink and hers blue, joined at roof level by a footbridge, the first modern houses in Mexico and a marriage diagrammed in concrete. In this year she paints nothing at all. There are three operations, an appendix, another lost pregnancy, and the discovery that Rivera is sleeping with her younger sister Cristina, who has been posing for him. She cuts off her hair. She takes an apartment in the centre and leaves the bridge standing.
suggested_refs: The Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo, San Ángel, by Juan O'Gorman
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

segments.name: The House That Took In Trotsky

stops.name: Casa Azul: Trotsky and Natalia Sedova
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the Trotskys reside at the Casa Azul 1937-1939
stops.campa: Rivera petitions Lázaro Cárdenas for asylum for a man no country will take, and Frida goes down to Tampico to meet the tanker. Leon Trotsky and Natalia Sedova move into the blue house; the windows onto the street are bricked up and armed men sit in the courtyard. Trotsky argued in Swiss cafés with a young socialist named Benito Mussolini before either of them had a country to lose. In Coyoacán he is fifty-seven and writes all day, and he and his hostess pass letters inside books. The affair lasts months. In 1939 he moves out, and in 1940 he is killed four streets away.
suggested_refs: The bricked-up windows of the Casa Azul, 1937; the Trotsky house on Avenida Viena
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
Bertram Wolfe, The Fabulous Life of Diego Rivera
mussolini.journey.json (the exile cafés of Lausanne; the forward link to Coyoacán is reconstruction)

stops.name: Mexico City: Breton comes to Mexico
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the phrase 'a ribbon around a bomb' belongs to Breton's New York catalogue essay of November 1938, not to this visit
stops.campa: André Breton arrives to see Trotsky and to find surrealism already living in the street. He finds it instead on the walls of the blue house and announces that Kahlo has been a surrealist all along without being told. She has not been. Two years earlier Antonin Artaud came through the same city hunting peyote and the sierra and a Mexico that would cure Europe, and wrote for El Nacional, and left with nothing but a habit. Breton leaves with paintings, a manifesto co-signed with Trotsky, and a phrase he will publish in New York in November.
suggested_refs: 'Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art', Breton, Trotsky and Rivera, Mexico 1938
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
artaud.journey.json (Mexico City, 1936)

stops.name: Casa Azul: four paintings to Edward G. Robinson
stops.date_confidence: summer 1938 attested; month reconstructed
stops.campa: The film actor Edward G. Robinson is holidaying in Mexico and buys four paintings at two hundred dollars each. It is the first money her own work has ever made, and it buys the one thing she has never had, which is the ability to go somewhere without asking Rivera for the fare. She writes to Ella Wolfe in New York that year in the voice she keeps for friends, which is filthy and does not apologize. By autumn she is packing for the first solo exhibition of her life, and she is going alone.
stops.quote: I drank because I wanted to drown my sorrows, but now the damned things have learned to swim.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Ella Wolfe, dated only 'Wednesday 13,' 1938; quoted in Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (1983), p. 197. The widely repeated date of 13 July 1938 is a downstream inference, not a documented one.
suggested_refs: The Kahlo-Wolfe correspondence, 1938
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
en.wikiquote.org, 'Frida Kahlo', citing Herrera

stops.name: Julien Levy Gallery: the ribbon around the bomb
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested
stops.campa: Twenty-five paintings go up on East 57th Street and about half of them sell. New York arrives to look at a Mexican woman in braids and rings who does not translate herself for anybody. Breton's catalogue essay supplies the sentence that will follow her for a century: that her art is a ribbon around a bomb. She is thirty-one, in a foreign city, unaccompanied and much photographed, and for the first time in her life the paintings on the wall are not there because of whom she married.
suggested_refs: Breton's catalogue essay, Julien Levy Gallery, November 1938
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Paris: the crossing
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested
stops.campa: She sails for France on Breton's promise of an exhibition and finds on arrival that nothing has been arranged, the paintings are still in customs, and the Breton household has no money and no hurry. She falls ill with a kidney infection. She stays among the surrealists and detests them: this bunch of coocoo lunatic sons of bitches, she writes home, who sit in cafés warming their precious behinds and talking without end about culture while the continent goes over the edge. She is in Paris seven months before the war begins.
suggested_refs: Kahlo's Paris letters of 1939, printed in Herrera
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
atlas canonical geography (Paris pin)

stops.name: Galerie Renou et Colle: Mexique
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the precise historical building is not independently confirmed, and the show is often misdescribed as a Kahlo solo exhibition
stops.campa: Marcel Duchamp, the only one of them she can stand, mounts the show after Breton fails to. It opens as Mexique: pre-Columbian figures, folk retablos, photographs by Manuel Álvarez Bravo, and seventeen paintings by Kahlo. Attendance is thin and the reviews are polite; Europe is six months from war and is thinking about that instead. Duchamp, Kandinsky and Picasso come and look properly. Picasso gives her a pair of tortoiseshell earrings shaped like hands and teaches her a Spanish song, and she keeps both for the rest of her life.
stops.quote: They thought I was a Surrealist, but I wasn't. I never painted dreams. I painted my own reality.
stops.quote_source: 'Mexican Autobiography,' Time magazine, 27 April 1953, on the surrealists' long-standing claim upon her work
suggested_refs: The exhibition 'Mexique', Galerie Renou et Colle, Paris, opened 10 March 1939
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
en.wikiquote.org, 'Frida Kahlo', citing Time

stops.name: Musée du Louvre: The Frame
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from the run of the exhibition
stops.campa: The Louvre buys The Frame, a self-portrait painted on aluminium behind a sheet of glass edged with birds and flowers in the manner of a village retablo. She becomes, by the account that follows the purchase, the first twentieth-century Mexican artist the museum has taken. The technique is one no French painter uses, because it is not a fine-art technique at all; it is what is done in Mexican markets to make an image of a saint. The picture is twenty-eight centimetres high.
suggested_refs: 'The Frame' (Le Cadre, c. 1938), Centre Pompidou, formerly Musée du Louvre
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Casa Azul: the petition and the two Fridas
stops.date_confidence: the petition is filed 6 November 1939; the decree is finalized in January 1940, and sources routinely compress both into a bare '1939'
stops.campa: Rivera asks for the divorce and she agrees to it, refuses his money, and moves back into the blue house she was born in. That winter she paints the largest canvas she will ever attempt: two women sitting side by side holding hands, one in the white lace of Europe with her heart cut open and an artery bleeding into her lap, one in Tehuana costume with the heart whole and a small portrait of Diego as a boy in her hand. A single vessel runs between them. Neither of the two women is looking at the other; both look out of the canvas.
suggested_refs: 'Las dos Fridas' (1939), painted at the Casa Azul during the divorce
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
Spanish Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: San Francisco: the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Eloesser gets her to San Francisco for treatment and tells Rivera plainly that she is dying of the separation and that he should marry her again. They remarry on Rivera's fifty-fourth birthday on terms she sets and states aloud: she will support herself out of her own earnings, the household costs will be halved, and there will be no sexual relations between them. She goes home to Coyoacán and he follows her there, into her father's house, and they live in it until she dies.
suggested_refs: The second marriage of Kahlo and Rivera, San Francisco, 8 December 1940
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Casa Azul: Guillermo Kahlo dies
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; exact day not established
stops.campa: Her father dies in the house he built. He is the one who photographed the colonial churches of Mexico for the government, who taught her to retouch a negative with a fine brush, who put her in a boys' preparatory school and told her to swim with the bad leg, and who came alone to the hospital in 1925. She paints his portrait years afterward with his camera beside him and the inscription that he was of German origin, an epileptic, and a man of genius. She has now buried both parents in the house where she was born.
suggested_refs: 'Retrato de mi padre Wilhelm Kahlo' (1951), Museo Frida Kahlo
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Casa Azul: the stepped pyramid
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Spanish Wikipedia gives 1941, correcting the widely repeated 1946); month not established
stops.campa: Rivera raises a small stepped pyramid in the garden of the blue house and sets his pre-Hispanic figures on its terraces, so that the courtyard where she keeps her monkeys, her parrots, her hairless dogs and her orange trees is presided over by stone gods dug out of the valley. She has been made a founding member of the Seminario de Cultura Mexicana and paints steadily now, mostly herself, at close range, with an animal at her shoulder. Rivera goes on buying pre-Hispanic figures by the crate, and the terraces fill up.
suggested_refs: The pyramid in the Casa Azul garden, built under Rivera's supervision, 1941
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Museo Frida Kahlo'
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: La Esmeralda: Los Fridos
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the 1940s campus location is approximate because the school later moved
stops.campa: She takes a teaching post at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado, called La Esmeralda, and finds she is good at it. She refuses to correct their drawing and takes them into the street instead, to markets and pulquerías and the walls of buildings, and tells them to paint what is there. Within months her back will not carry the journey, so four of them come out to Coyoacán and work in the garden under the pyramid. They are called Los Fridos. She gets them public walls to paint and pays for their materials out of her own fees.
suggested_refs: The murals of Los Fridos at the Pulquería La Rosita, Coyoacán
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Mexico City: the steel corset and The Broken Column
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the hospital's identity for this specific operation is not confirmed by all sources, and the coordinate is a reconstruction
stops.campa: Another spinal operation, and a steel corset she must wear for months. She paints the corsets while she is inside them, a hammer and sickle on one, an unborn child on another, and then she paints what the corset is holding: a body split open from throat to belly, the spine replaced by a cracked Ionic column, nails driven into the face and the arms and the thighs, the whole thing strapped shut with white bandages against an eroded desert. She is not lying down in the picture. She is standing up in it and looking straight out.
suggested_refs: 'La columna rota' (1944), Museo Dolores Olmedo
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Coyoacán: the interview with Antonio Rodríguez
stops.date_confidence: attested; the canonical Coyoacán pin of the atlas, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: Antonio Rodríguez comes out to the blue house for the magazine Así and asks her the question everyone asks, which is why she paints herself over and over. She gives the answer that will be reprinted in every language for eighty years, and it is not mystical and does not mention surrealism. It is an account of the working conditions of an invalid. In the same house, in the same barrio where Cortés quartered his men in 1521, she is running a studio out of a sickroom and describing it as a matter of who is available to sit.
stops.quote: I paint self-portraits because I am so often alone, because I am the person I know best.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Antonio Rodríguez, Así magazine, 17 March 1945
suggested_refs: Antonio Rodríguez's Así interview, 17 March 1945
sources: en.wikiquote.org, 'Frida Kahlo', citing Así
cortes.journey.json (Coyoacán, 1521)

stops.name: Mexico City: the prize for Moses
stops.date_confidence: year attested (English Wikipedia gives 1946, correcting a widely repeated 1945); month not established
stops.campa: The state gives her a national prize of five thousand pesos for Moses, a crowded panel she painted after reading Freud, with the infant in his basket at the centre of a sun and every god and hero and tyrant of the world ranked around him. It is the first official honour her country pays her, and it comes from the same government whose ministries her husband has been painting for twenty-five years. The following year the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes buys The Two Fridas for the nation, for four thousand pesos.
suggested_refs: 'Moisés' (1945), awarded the national prize in 1946
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
English Wikipedia, 'The Two Fridas'

stops.name: East 42nd Street, New York: the fusion of four vertebrae
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the address is the Hospital for Special Surgery's 1946 premises at 321 East 42nd Street, a reconstruction, since the pool's coordinate matched neither the 1946 nor the modern site
stops.campa: She goes north for a spinal fusion under Philip Wilson: four vertebrae joined, a graft taken from her pelvis, a metal rod set in. She spends two months on her back in New York and comes home in a steel corset with a promise of relief. It does not come. Within a year the graft is found to have been placed wrong, or to have failed, and the pain returns worse than before, along with the morphine that will not now leave her. Every operation after this one is an attempt to correct the last one.
suggested_refs: Philip Wilson's 1946 spinal fusion, Hospital for Special Surgery, New York
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo
English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Casa Azul: the year in bed
stops.date_confidence: the year in hospital runs 1950-1951; the date given is that of Gisèle Freund's article in Novedades
stops.campa: She spends the best part of a year in a Mexico City hospital after a bone graft turns septic and the surgeons go back in six or seven times, and Rivera takes the next bed and sleeps there. Then she is home in Coyoacán for good, in the bed with the mirror in its canopy, painting still lifes of split fruit with the easel swung over her. The photographer Gisèle Freund lives in the house for two years making pictures of her and prints in Novedades the sentence that arranges her whole life into two collisions.
stops.quote: I have suffered two grave accidents in my life, one in which a streetcar knocked me down. The other accident is Diego.
stops.quote_source: Gisèle Freund, 'Imagen de Frida Kahlo,' Novedades, 10 June 1951
suggested_refs: Gisèle Freund's photographs of Kahlo at the Casa Azul, 1950-1952
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

segments.name: The Bed Carried into the Gallery

stops.name: Galería de Arte Contemporáneo: the bed carried into the gallery
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the gallery's exact address on Amberes, in the Zona Rosa, is not independently verified
stops.campa: Lola Álvarez Bravo gives her the only solo exhibition she will ever have in her own country. Her doctors forbid her to leave the house. She has her four-poster bed dismantled, carried across the city, and installed in the gallery, and arrives after the doors open, on a stretcher, in an ambulance, with a motorcycle escort and a bell ringing. She is lifted into the bed and holds court in it all evening while two hundred people file past. The photographs of that night are reprinted for seventy years. She has eleven months left.
stops.quote: I am not sick. I am broken. But I am happy to be alive as long as I can paint.
suggested_refs: Lola Álvarez Bravo's Galería de Arte Contemporáneo, Amberes, Zona Rosa
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Frida Kahlo'
en.wikiquote.org, 'Frida Kahlo', citing Time

stops.name: Mexico City: the leg
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the hospital's identity and coordinate are a reconstruction
stops.campa: Gangrene takes the right foot, the foot of the polio leg, and the surgeons take the leg below the knee. She is fitted with a prosthesis and a red leather boot with bells on it, and for a while she practises walking and shows people the boot. Then she stops. In the diary she writes that she has wings instead of feet, and also that she wants to leave. The morphine goes up. Rivera later says she spent her last year in a state that was not sleeping and was not waking, and the paintings from this year are unsteady.
suggested_refs: Kahlo's prosthetic leg and red boot, Museo Frida Kahlo, exhibited from 2012
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Zócalo: the last time she is carried out
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the location is a reconstruction, given as a Mexico City demonstration rather than a documented square
stops.campa: Eleven days after leaving hospital with pneumonia she has herself put in a wheelchair and pushed into a Communist demonstration against the overthrow of Jacobo Árbenz in Guatemala by men the Central Intelligence Agency has armed. She sits in the crowd for four hours in the rain with a banner and a fist raised. It is the last time she is seen in public. Ten weeks later an Argentine doctor named Ernesto Guevara arrives in this city out of that same Guatemalan defeat, to photograph the plazas and wait, and never meets her.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Kahlo at the 2 July 1954 demonstration, her last public appearance
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Casa Azul: the exit
stops.date_confidence: attested; pulmonary embolism is the official cause, and the suspicion of an overdose, recorded by her nurse and by later biographers, has never been confirmed
stops.campa: She dies in the night in the bed she was born a few rooms from, one week past her forty-seventh birthday. The certificate says pulmonary embolism. Her nurse counts the pills and finds too few, and says so, and no autopsy is performed. The last drawing in the diary is a black angel rising, and beneath it a line she wrote days before. Rivera says afterwards that it was the most tragic day of his life, and that he understood too late that the best part of him had been her.
stops.quote: I hope the exit is joyful and I hope never to return.
stops.quote_source: Frida Kahlo's diary, final entry, July 1954
suggested_refs: The last page of Kahlo's diary, Museo Frida Kahlo
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes: the flag on the coffin
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources disagree on whether the flag is that of the Mexican Communist Party or the Soviet Union, and the disagreement is left standing
stops.campa: The body lies in state in the marble hall of the national palace of fine arts, and a former party official lays a flag with hammer and sickle over the coffin. Rivera stands beside it and does not have it removed. Six hundred people file past in the state institution of a government that has spent thirty years managing its own revolution. The scandal takes a year to be paid for, and it is not Rivera who pays it: the director of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes, Andrés Iduarte, is dismissed in 1955 for having permitted the flag.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the lying in state, Palacio de Bellas Artes, 14 July 1954
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Panteón Civil de Dolores: the furnace
stops.date_confidence: the cremation is attested; the upright-corpse account is tradition transmitted through witnesses, and this coordinate standardizes three conflicting values carried in the research pool
stops.campa: She is taken to the civil cemetery of Dolores to be burned, as she asked, having said she had lain down enough. The mourners are singing when the trolley runs into the furnace. Those standing closest, the poet Andrés Henestrosa among them, say that the heat contracted the body and lifted it upright inside the fire with the hair burning around the head like a crown, and that it sat up and faced them before it went. Rivera draws the scene in his notebook. The ashes are gathered an hour later, still warm, into a bag.
suggested_refs: Andrés Henestrosa's account of the cremation, transmitted through Herrera
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (account tagged as tradition)

stops.name: Casa Azul: the house becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; the house is conveyed by the Fideicomiso de los Museos Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo, created in 1957 and administered by the Banco de México, not by a will
stops.campa: Rivera puts the blue house and everything in it into a trust for the Mexican people and dies in November 1957. Eight months later the house opens as the Museo Frida Kahlo, with the kitchen as she left it, the easel over the bed, the corsets, the retablos, and the pre-Hispanic figures on the garden pyramid. Her ashes stay in the bedroom, in a pre-Columbian urn shaped like a toad, on the bed she died in. She has no grave. The bedroom is on the visitor route, and the urn stays on the bed while the queue goes past it.
suggested_refs: The Fideicomiso de los Museos Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo, 1957

stops.name: Casa Azul: the sealed bathrooms
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the specific month of the opening is not established
stops.campa: Rivera ordered a bathroom and several storerooms of the house locked and left shut for fifteen years after his own death. They stay shut for fifty. When they are opened, out come six thousand photographs, twelve thousand documents, three hundred garments, the plaster corsets, the prosthetic leg with its red boot, and the letters. By then Hayden Herrera's biography has remade her, a film has been made, her face is on the five-hundred-peso note, and her name is a trademark her family is suing over. The garments are catalogued for eight years before any of them goes on show.
suggested_refs: The 2004 opening of the sealed Casa Azul archive; the exhibition 'Las Apariencias Engañan'
